Vendor

Vendor
A market vendor at a stall

In a supply chain, a vendor, or a seller, is an enterprise that contributes goods or services. Generally, a supply chain vendor manufactures inventory or stock items and sells them to the next link in the chain. Today, these terms refer to a supplier of any good or service. In retail and everyday usage, "vendor" also denotes a person who sells goods directly to the public, for example from a market stall, cart or vending machine.

Roles in the supply chain

Vendors occupy various positions: manufacturers sell to distributors or wholesalers, who in turn sell to retailers, who sell to end customers. In business-to-business commerce, companies manage their vendors through procurement processes, vendor qualification, contracts and service-level agreements. In information technology, a vendor is a company that sells hardware, software or services — examples include large software vendors whose products may create vendor lock-in for their customers.

Types of vendor

  • Street vendors sell food, drinks or small goods in public places and form a large part of the informal economy in many cities worldwide.
  • Market vendors trade from stalls in markets and fairs.
  • Third-party vendors supply goods or services to a company under contract, such as catering, cleaning or IT support.
  • Vendor of record – in some procurement and staffing arrangements, the single approved intermediary through which other suppliers must work.

Vendor management

Organisations practise vendor management to select suppliers, negotiate terms, monitor performance and manage risk, including dependence on a single source. In real estate and law, the "vendor" is simply the party selling property, as opposed to the purchaser.
